source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Founding paper of rational analysis of memory. Ebbinghaus's retention and practice data fit power functions, not exponentials. This sets the target the theory must explain.
numbers: Ebbinghaus retention: log P = 3.862 - 0.126 log delay, R2=.978 (delays 20 min to 31 days). Practice (days of study): log trials = 4.08 - 1.44 log days, R2=.996, versus exponential-form fit R2=.949 on the same data.
limits: Ebbinghaus used one subject and only 1-6 days of practice, so the range cannot separate power from exponential cleanly. The authors admit this.
agent_relevance: Memory strength should be modelled as a power law in time since use, not an exponential. Exponential decay (as in simple agent memory stores) is the wrong default.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Core claim: the probability that a memory is needed in the world follows the same statistics as memory availability. They counted real 'demands' on memory in three sources and predicted day/utterance 101 from the previous 100.
numbers: Sources: 730 days of New York Times headlines (1 Jan 1986 - 31 Dec 1987); the CHILDES child-language database (parental speech); the first author's e-mail, Mar 1985 - Dec 1989 (senders). Need probability = k x past proportion, with k = 1.0 (NYT), .76 (parent speech), .9 (e-mail). k reflects how often new items appear.
limits: Three corpora only, one person's e-mail, and word headlines are a loose stand-in for 'memory demand'. Log-odds vs log-frequency is linear only below frequency about 50; a few function words and two e-mail senders lie above the line and are set aside.
agent_relevance: Frequency of past use is a legitimate predictor of future need. A ranking rule built on use counts has a principled basis, but only in sources that look like these.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Environmental retention functions are power laws. Log need-odds is linear in log time since last occurrence, and not exponential.
numbers: Power exponents: .73 (NYT), .77 (child language), .83 (e-mail). Authors state exponential did not fit in any of the three.
limits: Exponent about .7-.8 in the world is larger than the exponent of .126 in the Ebbinghaus lab data. The paper attributes some gaps to item frequency and pattern-of-use confounds, not fully resolved.
agent_relevance: Recency weight should fall slowly (power law). A fast exponential recency decay throws away useful old memories.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Spacing effect appears in the environment too. The retention slope is steeper when the two prior uses were close together than when they were far apart (a Glenberg 1976 analog).
numbers: Retention exponent by prior-use lag, short vs long: NYT .49 vs .20; parental speech .76 vs .45; e-mail 1.03 vs .48. Items used exactly twice in the prior 100 days were analysed.
limits: Natural-corpus lag analysis is correlational. Number of prior uses is controlled only by choosing items used exactly twice.
agent_relevance: Items used repeatedly over spread-out times should be kept longer than items hit in one burst. A flat use counter misses this.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: Practice and retention combine about additively in log-odds scales. This holds in lab data (Hellyer 1962, Krueger 1929, Underwood & Keppel 1963) and in the NYT and child-language corpora split by item frequency.
numbers: Hellyer: 1-8 presentations, delays 3-27 s. Krueger: 12 nouns, overlearning, 1-28 days. Underwood & Keppel: nine letter associates, 1 or 7 days.
limits: Authors say they have 'no investment' in true additivity, only approximate agreement. They also note the simple prediction that forgetting and practice exponents sum to 1 found no support in the Ebbinghaus data.
agent_relevance: Score = f(use history) + g(time since use) can be combined by addition on a log scale. A simple additive score is defensible.

source: Anderson & Schooler (1991) Reflections of the environment in memory
finding: The formal model: (0) trace strength encodes need odds; (1) strengths from separate presentations sum; (2) each presentation decays as a power function of time; (3) the decay exponent shrinks as time since the previous presentation grows. Assumption 3 is what produced the spacing effect here.
numbers: Illustrated by practice functions with initial decay d1=.125 (log S = -1.98 + 0.84 log D, R2=1.000) and d1=1.000 (log S = -11.60 + 0.31 log D, R2=.964).
limits: Assumption 3 depends only on lag from the last presentation. Pavlik & Anderson later replaced it because it did not handle massed-practice conditions.
agent_relevance: This is the root of the base-level learning equation B = ln(sum t_j^-d). It is the formula to copy when ranking stored items.

source: Anderson & Milson (1989) Human memory: an adaptive perspective (cited in Anderson & Schooler 1991)
finding: Earlier rational analysis used mathematical models of library borrowings and computer file access to predict need. Anderson & Schooler say it had two weaknesses: the sources were not human memory demands, and the formal model hid the direct environment-memory link.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Known only through the 1991 description; not opened.
agent_relevance: Backward citation for the idea that retrieval ranking should track the statistics of future need.

source: Pavlik & Anderson (2004) An ACT-R model of the spacing effect
finding: Spacing experiment on Japanese-English paired associates. Spacing helped more the more repetitions there were. More forgetting after 7 days than 1 day.
numbers: N=40 (20 per retention group), 104 word pairs, 8 pairs per condition. Session 1 repeats 1,2,4,8 times at lags 2,14,98 trials (8x98 dropped, 11 conditions). Retest after 1 or 7 days. Session-2 correctness .64 (1 day) vs .52 (7 days). Spacing main effect F(2,76)=58.2; repetition x spacing F(4,152)=4.38, p<.05.
limits: Only 20 per group, one stimulus type, words learned by non-Japanese speakers. This is the 2004 conference version, not the 2005 Cognitive Science paper.
agent_relevance: Spaced reuse, not just reuse count, drives later retrievability. A use counter should weight gaps.

source: Pavlik & Anderson (2004) An ACT-R model of the spacing effect
finding: New ACT-R mechanism: the decay rate of each trace depends on the activation at the time it was laid down (high activation then, faster decay), not on a fixed d. This yields the spacing effect and its interaction with practice.
numbers: Fit to 162 data points: RMSD=.046, r2=.971, but chi-square=260 on 157 df. Parameters: decay intercept a=.167, scale c=.232, noise s=.252, threshold tau=-.669, intervening-events h=.031. Second test on Glenberg (1976) exp 3 (recognition of consonant trigrams, lags 0-40, delays 8/32/64): r2=.980, RMSD=.009 with a=.104, c=.374, s=.4.
limits: The chi-square of 260 on 157 df is a statistical misfit. The model failed on the 8-repetition, lag-14 condition, where humans gained a large spacing benefit it could not reproduce; authors suggest a non-declarative process. Parameters were refitted for the second data set.
agent_relevance: Adaptive decay (items retrieved when still strong age faster) is a candidate refinement over fixed d=0.5, but it costs several extra parameters.

source: Pavlik & Anderson (2004) An ACT-R model of the spacing effect
finding: Open dispute about the form of decay: power function (favoured by Newell & Rosenbloom 1981, Wixted & Ebbesen 1997, Anderson & Schooler 1991) versus exponential (Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort 2000; Myung, Kim & Pitt 2000). Authors keep the power law because it matches environment statistics and is parsimonious.
numbers: No numbers; argument only.
limits: Heathcote et al. and Myung et al. were not opened; this line relays the Pavlik & Anderson paragraph. The averaging-artifact argument (averaging exponentials looks like a power law) is a real competing explanation.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the power law is settled; test both recency forms on our own data.

source: Anderson, Fincham & Douglass (1999) Practice and retention: a unifying analysis
finding: Strength accumulation equation: strength = sum of t_j^-d over all past practices. It predicts the power law of practice and the power law of retention from one function. Fitted to 5 experiments with up to 240 practice trials and gaps up to 400 days.
numbers: Experiment 1 fit: d=.52, A=3.54 s, H=7.02 blocks, R2=.974; prediction SD 1.01 s vs standard error 1.12 s. Strength rises from 2.26 (block 1) to 19.33 (end), about 10x, matching latency 35 s to 7 s. Experiment 3 (practice with gaps up to a year): overall correlation .941; correlation of predicted vs observed warm-up decrements .95.
limits: Fits are to latency in one fact-and-rule paradigm (sports events with day/hour rules), small groups (Exp 4 had 5 participants per cell). The model needed the extra clock-slowing parameter H.
agent_relevance: Direct support for ranking by a sum of power-law-decayed uses. d about .5 is a defensible default.

source: Anderson, Fincham & Douglass (1999) Practice and retention: a unifying analysis
finding: 'Slowed clock': time outside the experiment counts for less than clock time. Between sessions items age far less than during a session. Anderson (1982) predicted that the practice exponent equals 1 - d, and this held.
numbers: Items age 32 blocks within a session but only 9.59 blocks between sessions in the earlier Anderson & Fincham (1994) data; H estimates near 12 blocks per day in later experiments. Power fit to that data: 3.38 + 11.35 n^-.41, matching 1 - .60. The simple power fit explains about 2% less variance (R2 .966) than the strength equation, mainly missing start-of-day warm-up losses.
limits: The authors say clock time may be the wrong variable and that number of intervening events may be the true one. This is an unresolved competing account.
agent_relevance: Time-based decay in an agent should perhaps count events (turns, tasks) between uses, not wall-clock time.

source: Anderson, Fincham & Douglass (1999) Practice and retention: a unifying analysis
finding: Spacing explanation: if a day's rest is worth H blocks, massing more than about 2H blocks gives items that are 'accelerating forgetting', so splitting practice over two days wins. Authors say this is only a contributing factor to the spacing effect.
numbers: Predicted crossover near 2H (about 24-48 blocks). Exp 4 compared 24 vs 48 blocks per day over 4 days, 8 groups of 5 participants. Training condition latency: examples only 15.31 s, rule only 12.35 s, example+rule 10.88 s, no prior training 10.66 s.
limits: Exp 4 groups are tiny (n=5). I did not read the transfer table, so the result of the spacing prediction is not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Spreading repeated retrieval over sessions is the cheap way to harden stored knowledge.

source: Anderson, Fincham & Douglass (1999) Practice and retention: a unifying analysis
finding: Debates on functional form named in the paper: Heathcote & Mewhort (1995) say including the intercept can favour exponentials; Anderson & Tweney (1997) and Myung et al. say averaging exponentials mimics power laws; Rickard (1997) says the power law of practice holds only approximately and only for some tasks.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Cited arguments only; the cited works were not opened.
agent_relevance: Record as a standing counter-hypothesis.

source: Anderson, Reder & Lebiere (1996) Working memory: activation limitations on retrieval
finding: Gives the ACT-R activation equations. Activation is the sum of source activation times association strength: A_i = sum W_j S_ji. Retrieval odds = C e^(cA); retrieval time = B e^(-bA). The working memory limit is a fixed total source activation shared between concurrent tasks.
numbers: Experiment 1: 15 participants (CMU students and staff); Experiment 2: 20 participants. Task: hold a digit span (2/4/6 digits in Exp 1) while solving an algebra equation, then recall digits. Span effect on equation accuracy, F(2,28)=4.96, p<.05; Exp 2 span-recall main effects F(3,57)=35.87 and equation complexity F(1,19)=46.75, both p<.001.
limits: Base-level activation is set to zero in this paper (footnote 2), so it tests spreading activation and not use-history. Samples are small.
agent_relevance: Loading the context with many cues lowers the activation of each one. Cue overload in a prompt is the analog.

source: Anderson, Reder & Lebiere (1996) Working memory: activation limitations on retrieval
finding: The fixed-capacity single-pool model beat a separate-capacity alternative. In Exp 1 the seven-parameter separate-capacity model fit worse and could not explain the effect of equation complexity on digit recall. In Exp 2 the separate model fit about as well but needed two extra parameters.
numbers: Exp 1: separate-capacity chi-square=36.14, about 10 higher than the original with two fewer parameters. Exp 2: separate-capacity chi-square=79.7, similar fit, +2 parameters. Carlson et al. (1989) as cited: memory load 3 vs 6 cost 35 ms on non-access trials and 296 ms on access trials.
limits: In Exp 2 time-decay could account for part of the complexity effect, so the evidence for a pure activation account is mixed; the authors say Exp 1 casts doubt on time as the cause.
agent_relevance: Retrieval degradation is graded, not a hard capacity wall. Match to LLM context overload.

source: Lebiere, Anderson & Reder (1994) Error modeling in the ACT-R production system
finding: Declarative errors come in two kinds. Omission: a chunk cannot reach the retrieval threshold in time (modelled with a latency cutoff and Gaussian activation noise). Commission: a wrong chunk is retrieved because partial matching lets a more active, partly matching chunk beat the correct one after a mismatch penalty.
numbers: Human data: simple vs complex equations solved 96.9% vs 90.8%; memory load 2/4/6 solved 95.2/94.7/91.7%; digit strings recalled 95.0% (simple eq.) vs 91.3% (complex), and 95.5/95.8/88.1% for 2/4/6 digits. Of equation errors, 125 (61%) were algebraic transformations and 17 (8%) arithmetic.
limits: Most errors were wrong-but-related items, not blanks. The model was fitted to a single algebra-plus-digit-span task. Counts come from one conference paper and were not replicated here.
agent_relevance: LLM memory errors look like commission errors (a near-match item wins). Ranking should expect confusable neighbours, not only misses.

source: Lovett, Daily & Reder (2000) A source activation theory of working memory: cross-task prediction of performance in ACT-R
finding: One free parameter W (total source activation) varies across people, normally distributed around 1.0, and fits each person's serial-position curves on a modified digit span task. With W fixed, it predicts the same person's n-back results.
numbers: Link between MODS-estimated W and n-back accuracy: r=0.04 (p=.92) in the group that said they used an activation strategy; r=.56 (p=.12) in the update-strategy group. Group sizes small (not recorded in the text I read).
limits: The cross-task link was not significant in either strategy group. Strategy differences complicate the single-parameter story.
agent_relevance: Individual differences in cue capacity are a boundary condition; one memory setting will not be right for every task.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior
finding: Retrieval ranks memory objects by recency + importance + relevance, each min-max scaled to [0,1] and summed. Recency is exponential decay by game hours since last retrieval; importance is an integer 1-10 asked from the LLM; relevance is embedding similarity to the query.
numbers: Recency decay factor 0.995 per game hour. Weights stated to be equal in the paper (the extracted text was cut off, so this is from memory of the paper). 25 agents, 2 game days. Believability (TrueSkill): full 29.89 (sigma .72), no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowd-worker 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<.001; full vs fully ablated d = 8.16. 100 rank sets.
limits: The ablations remove whole memory types, not individual scoring terms, so the retrieval formula itself is not isolated. Authors report agents fail to retrieve and embellish.
agent_relevance: This is the baseline an ACT-R-style rule must beat. It lacks a frequency term and uses exponential, not power-law, recency.

source: Park et al. (2023) vs ACT-R base-level activation (analysis)
finding: Mapping: relevance corresponds to spreading activation. Recency corresponds to base-level decay, but in Park it is exponential and keyed to the last retrieval, so repeated use is not counted. Importance has no direct ACT-R counterpart.
numbers: Park: 0.995 per hour. ACT-R: B = ln(sum t_j^-d), d about .5 (Anderson et al. 1999 fitted .52, and later used .50).
limits: This is my comparison, not a result either paper tested. No paper I opened ran Park scoring against ACT-R scoring head to head.
agent_relevance: A cheap test: add a use-count power-law term to the retrieval score and compare to recency-only on our own tasks.

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MemoryBank: enhancing LLMs with long-term memory
finding: Forgetting is an Ebbinghaus-style exponential: R = e^(-t/S). S starts at 1 on first mention, goes up by 1 on each recall, and t resets to 0. Authors call it an 'exploratory and highly simplified' model.
numbers: Test set: 194 probing questions (97 English, 97 Chinese). Metrics: retrieval accuracy, response correctness (0/.5/1), coherence, ranking score. Three SiliconFriend variants (ChatGLM, BELLE, ChatGPT). Table 2 values were not cleanly extractable from the text I read.
limits: Exponential, not power-law. I found no ablation of the forgetting rule against no-forgetting in the text I read, so a benefit of the forgetting rule itself was not found.
agent_relevance: Frequency-reset-on-recall is a crude proxy for ACT-R use history. No measured gain from it is shown.

source: Alqithami (2025) Forgetful but Faithful: MaRS and FiFA benchmark
finding: Six forgetting policies (FIFO, LRU, Priority Decay, Reflection-Summary, Random-Drop, Hybrid) over 300 simulated runs and 5 budgets. Abstract and body disagree on which wins.
numbers: Abstract: Hybrid best, composite 0.911. Body Table 2: Random Drop best 0.635 +-0.024, then FIFO 0.602 +-0.012 and Priority Decay 0.601 +-0.021; Random Drop goal completion only 0.078 +-0.010. Composite weights: coherence .25, goal .25, social recall .20, privacy .15, cost .15.
limits: Simulated, not human data, and the composite rewards cheap policies that avoid social references. The internal inconsistency lowers trust. Not an ACT-R test; no base-level activation policy was run.
agent_relevance: Warns that composite scores can crown a bad forgetting policy. Report goal completion separately.

source: Aschenbrenner, Heisler, Sievers & Becker-Asano (2026) Not Forgotten: personalized episodic memory for the humanoid robot head Kim
finding: Retrieval = cosine similarity + a memory strength score built from creation age, access count (log), last-access recency and emotional intensity. This is an ACT-R-like use-history idea, but with linear and log terms, not the ACT-R power law.
numbers: S(m)=3.0*max(0,1-0.1*t_creation)+2.0*ln(1+N_access)+1.5*max(0,1-0.05*t_last_access), times an emotion multiplier. Within-subject video study N=43 (52 began): sociability d=0.60, p<.001; trustworthy d=.62; warm d=.56; disturbance d=0.00; 27 of 43 (63%) preferred the memory system, not significant.
limits: The test is memory vs no memory in a video, not scoring rule vs scoring rule. The weights 3.0/2.0/1.5 were not tuned against alternatives, and the forgetting mechanism was not validated.
agent_relevance: Shows a use-count log term is easy to add. It gives no evidence that this term is better than plain similarity.

source: Sievers & Russwinkel (2025) Personalized interactions with a social robot based on recollections from a cognitive model
finding: Real ACT-R (pyactr) declarative memory holds chunks written by gpt-4o-mini (person name, keywords, fact phrase, date). Retrieved chunks are pasted into the LLM prompt. Task selection is also by chunks.
numbers: Proof of concept only. Authors: task selection and person model work 'with an unsatisfactory level of reliability'; 'a detailed quantitative evaluation is still pending'.
limits: No measured result. Retrieval is influenced by noise and utility but those were not studied.
agent_relevance: The only implementation I found that runs true ACT-R activation under an LLM. It has no data yet, so it is a design pointer, not evidence.

source: Kerestecioglu et al. (2026) Human-inspired memory architecture for LLM agents
finding: Importance-score decay for pruning (exponential, lambda=0.001 per hour, half-life 29 days) plus consolidation, on a VSCode issue stream and on LongMemEval. Forgetting and consolidation hurt on LongMemEval except at a very large budget.
numbers: VSCode: 97.2% retention precision, 58% store reduction, +21.8 pp over keep-everything (75.4%). LongMemEval S-tier overall: raw RAG 78.4% [74.8,82.0]; dedup-only 76.8; adaptive-10K 57.0; aggressive consolidation 48.4 [44.0,52.8]. M-tier overall: raw RAG 71.2% [67.2,75.0]; pipeline at 200K tokens 70.1 [66.0,74.2]; 115K 65.6; 50K 49.2; 25K 38.8. Single-session preference +13.3 pp (56.7 to 70.0) with only 30 questions.
limits: Single run with bootstrap CIs; authors say maturation and reconsolidation were not tested because LongMemEval lacks repeated retrieval over weeks. No ACT-R terms. Decay was tuned on their own synthetic data.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-evidence: on an accuracy benchmark, forgetting by score never beat keeping everything and retrieving well. Ranking should reorder, not delete.

source: Uddin et al. (2026) From recall to forgetting: benchmarking long-term memory for personalized agents
finding: A benchmark that stresses memory consolidation and frequent knowledge updates rather than plain fact retrieval. It does not test ACT-R activation as far as the passages I scanned show.
numbers: Only the abstract and related-work text were scanned; no scores recorded.
limits: Not read in full, so no claims about results.
agent_relevance: Candidate test set for a use-history ranking rule, because it needs updates and forgetting.

source: pensyve-core (2025-26) activation.rs, open-source agent-memory code
finding: A practitioner library implements the ACT-R base-level formula B = ln(sum (t - t_k)^-d) for agent memories. Its tests check recent accesses score higher than old ones.
numbers: No benchmark numbers (search snippet only).
limits: Search result only, not opened. Blog and Reddit reports of gains are anecdotal.
agent_relevance: Shows the formula is already used in agent stacks without published measured gains.
